notes.b: Genes that sit on the same chromosome are passed on together, because a chromosome goes into a gamete as one piece. This is called linkage.
points: Each chromosome carries many genes in a fixed order along one DNA molecule, and a chromosome passes into a gamete (a sex cell) as one unit, so any two genes on it travel together.
Linked genes are not joined to each other in any special way. They are simply on the same DNA molecule, which is why they are inherited together.
All the genes on one chromosome form a linkage group, so there are as many linkage groups as there are chromosome pairs.

Linked genotypes show the alleles (versions of a gene) on each chromosome together, with a line or slash for the pair of chromosomes. AB/ab means one chromosome carries A and B and its homologue (the matching chromosome of the pair) carries a and b.
Diagram: two vertical bars (a homologous pair), one labelled with A above B, the other with a above b, at matching positions; label “homologous chromosomes”, “linked genes” and “locus”.
notes.tip: If asked what linkage means, say that genes on the same chromosome are inherited together. Do not confuse it with sex-linkage, which is about genes on a sex chromosome.

notes.h: How linkage affects independent assortment (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Independent assortment means the alleles of one gene are sorted into gametes without affecting the alleles of another gene. That only works if the genes are on separate chromosomes, so linkage is an exception to it.
points: The Law of Independent Assortment holds only for genes on different chromosomes. The Law of Segregation still applies to each gene, so linkage is an exception to one law, not a refutation of Mendel.
Linked genes do not assort independently: the alleles on one chromosome move together into the same gamete when the homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis (the cell division that makes gametes).
A double heterozygote (heterozygous for both genes) with linked genes, AB/ab, produces only two types of gamete, AB and ab, in equal numbers.

An unlinked double heterozygote produces four types (AB, Ab, aB, ab) instead. The gametes Ab and aB (new combinations) are not formed when the genes are linked, because A and B stay together on one chromosome.
Offspring show only (or mostly) the parental combinations of traits, while the new combinations seen with unlinked genes are missing (or rare).
So linkage gives fewer types of offspring and less variation, and the ratios differ from 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 and 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.

In real organisms, linked genes are occasionally separated, so a small number of offspring with new combinations can appear. The reason is crossing over, and genes are more likely to stay together the closer they lie on the chromosome.

Diagram: side by side, (a) unlinked genes: two chromosome pairs (A/a on one, B/b on the other) giving four gamete types AB, Ab, aB, ab; (b) linked genes: one chromosome pair, A and B on one homologue, a and b on the other, giving two gamete types AB and ab.
notes.tip: To explain why linked genes do not obey independent assortment, say that the alleles on one chromosome go into the same gamete together. For how a linked cross differs, give mostly parental phenotypes, few or no new combinations, less variation, and not the expected ratio.

notes.h: Worked example: test cross with linked genes (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A test cross mates an individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive one, so the offspring reveal which gametes it makes. With linked genes, only two kinds of offspring appear.
points: Key: A = dominant allele of gene 1, a = recessive; B = dominant allele of gene 2, b = recessive; A and B on the same chromosome.
Parents' phenotypes: AB/ab shows both dominant traits; ab/ab shows both recessive traits. Parents' genotypes: AB/ab × ab/ab.
Gametes: AB, ab × ab. The recessive parent can only give ab, so each offspring's type shows which gamete came from the other parent.
Offspring genotypes: AB/ab (AaBb) and ab/ab (aabb), 1 : 1. Offspring phenotypes: 1 showing both dominant traits : 1 showing both recessive traits.
If the genes were unlinked, the same cross (AaBb × aabb) would give four phenotypes, 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Linkage removes the two new combinations.

The arrangement matters. If the double heterozygote has the dominant allele of one gene with the recessive allele of the other on each chromosome (Ab/aB), its gametes are Ab and aB, and the test cross gives 1 Aabb : 1 aaBb, i.e. only the two mixed phenotypes.
Always read which alleles are on the same chromosome, because AB/ab and Ab/aB are different genotypes that give different offspring.
notes.tip: Write the genotype with a slash first, then list only the gametes that keep each chromosome together.

notes.h: Worked example: F1 × F1 with linked genes (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Crossing two linked double heterozygotes (the F1, or first-generation offspring) shows how linkage changes the familiar dihybrid ratio.
points: Parents: AB/ab × AB/ab.
Gametes: AB, ab × AB, ab. Each parent makes only two gamete types because the genes are linked.
Punnett square: AB/AB, AB/ab / AB/ab, ab/ab.
Offspring genotypes: 1 AABB : 2 AaBb : 1 aabb.
Phenotypes: 3 both dominant : 1 both recessive (3 : 1), compared with 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 if the genes were unlinked, because no offspring show a dominant and a recessive trait together.
notes.tip: A 3 : 1 ratio from a dihybrid cross, instead of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, is the sign of linkage. Quote 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 only as the comparison.

notes.h: A real example: Drosophila melanogaster (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The fruit fly gives a real case of two genes inherited together. Both genes sit on the same chromosome, so the results of a test cross do not match the unlinked pattern.
points: In the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, the genes for body colour (grey dominant to black) and wing shape (normal wings dominant to vestigial wings) are on the same chromosome.

A test cross of a fly heterozygous for both (with grey and normal on one chromosome) with a black, vestigial fly gives mostly grey normal-winged and black vestigial-winged offspring, the parental combinations.
Only a few grey vestigial or black normal flies appear, not the 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 expected for unlinked genes, because the genes are usually inherited together.
notes.tip: Use this example to show that real results are mostly parental types with a few new combinations. You do not need numbers.

notes.h: Recognising linkage from results (Higher Level only)
notes.b: In an exam you may be given offspring results and asked whether the genes are linked. You decide by comparing them with the ratios expected for unlinked genes.
points: A dihybrid cross (a cross following two genes) whose offspring show mainly the parental combinations suggests that the two genes are linked.

Fewer phenotype classes than expected, or a ratio far from 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (F1 × F1) or 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (test cross), also suggests that the two genes are linked, because linked alleles stay together instead of mixing.
notes.tip: To explain how a dihybrid cross's results would differ if the genes were linked, name three things: mostly parental phenotypes, few or no new combinations, and less variation.

questions.prompt: A fruit fly heterozygous for body colour and wing shape is test-crossed. Most offspring resemble one or other parent. Explain this result.
questions.model: The genes for body colour and wing shape are on the same chromosome, so they are linked and do not assort independently. The fly's alleles on each chromosome are inherited together, so most offspring show the parental combinations: grey normal-winged or black vestigial-winged. The few offspring with other combinations arise because linked genes are occasionally separated, as a result of crossing over, so they are rare rather than the 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 expected for unlinked genes.
